personality_traits: exasperated but conflict-avoidant - voices frustration only as a bewildered question rather than a demand
anxious/fidgety under pressure, shown wringing his fingers rather than raising his voice
passive in the scene - stands holding a coat and reacting rather than initiating action
expressions: 0:00 neutral, slightly worried brow while holding the coat and eyeing the pile of shopping bags
0:01-0:05 eyebrows raised, eyes wide behind slipping glasses as he asks 'How is that even possible?' - mouth open in a flat, incredulous line
0:07-0:10 close-up reaction shot: eyes drop, mouth tightens into a small downturned frown while his wife delivers the 'it's not supposed to make sense' line off him
throughout: glasses perpetually sliding to the tip of his long nose, giving a permanently tired, put-upon look
gestures: holds a second black coat draped over one forearm for the entire scene, never sets it down
stands stiffly upright near the open closet, body angled toward the bed
rubs/wrings his fingertips together nervously (visible close-up) as the punchline lands
head tilts slightly back when reacting to 'possible?', a small recoil rather than a big gesture
characters.interactions_notes: Paul is staged on the left, physically separated from his wife by the clothes-piled bed, and is mostly shown in isolated reaction shots (medium shot and extreme close-up) rather than in a two-shot conversing with her. He initiates the complaint but the camera keeps returning to his face for his wife's dialogue, framing him as the butt of the joke - his anxious fidgeting plays under her line rather than his own. There is no sustained eye contact between the two; each looks mostly toward their own activity (his hands/her bags) rather than at each other, reinforcing a low-communication, passive-aggressive marital dynamic that the episode title card ('Men Will Never Understand') frames as the whole point of the joke.

personality_traits: unbothered and self-assured - treats an irrational-seeming purchase as perfectly logical
mildly dismissive/patronizing toward her husband, using his first name pointedly ('It's fashion, Paul')
content and absorbed in her own activity (sorting new clothes) rather than engaging with his concern
expressions: 0:00 relaxed, slightly pleased look while pulling clothes out of shopping bags on the bed
0:03-0:05 flat, unimpressed half-lidded eyes as she half-listens to his complaint, no visible worry
0:07-0:10 deadpan, faint smirk while delivering 'It's fashion, Paul. It's not supposed to make sense.' - eyebrows barely raised, as if stating the obvious
gestures: sits cross-legged on the bed surrounded by shopping bags, sorting through them the entire scene
holds up individual clothing items (a dark top, then a burgundy piece) to inspect them, unbothered by the surrounding mess
keeps hands busy with the bags rather than gesturing toward her husband, signaling she isn't taking his complaint seriously
characters.interactions_notes: The wife stays seated on the bed throughout, physically higher and more settled in the frame than her pacing/standing husband, giving her a visual position of calm control. She delivers the episode's punchline directly by name ('Paul'), the only moment of direct verbal address between them, which lands as gently condescending. She never turns her body fully toward him or drops what she's doing, reinforcing that she is unmoved by his exasperation - the comedic power dynamic is her nonchalance versus his mounting, silent anxiety.
